title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on standalone numeral tokens (often followed by a period or bolding markdown) that mark the start of an item in an enumerated or numbered list, such as '3.', '4.', or '2. **'. The activating tokens are the list index numbers themselves, not the content that follows them, appearing across a wide range of topics and list lengths. It is not sensitive to the semantic content of the list items, the specific number value, or narrative counting within prose -- it specifically tracks the formatting role of a numeral as a list delimiter/enumerator, distinguishing it from numbers used as quantities, dates, or measurements in running text.

title: Empathetic exclamatory validation opener
description: This latent fires on formulaic opening exclamations or statements that validate the emotional or situational difficulty of what a user has described, typically in an advice-giving context (e.g., 'What a complex and sensitive situation!', 'That can be a really tough and confusing experience.'). The highest-activating examples are almost all templated 'What a [adjective] and [adjective] situation/feeling/topic!' exclamations paired with two empathy-signaling adjectives (challenging, sensitive, complex, painful, emotional, etc.), serving as a rapport-building preamble before substantive advice. The broader cluster extends to related empathetic validation phrases like 'It's understandable that...' or 'That's completely understandable!' which acknowledge feelings without yet giving content. It does NOT include the substantive advice, analysis, or reasoning that follows these openers, nor does it activate on sentences that merely describe a difficult situation without this validating, empathetic framing (e.g., neutral factual descriptions or direct advice statements).

title: AITA-style verdict framing
description: This latent fires on the r/AmItheAsshole genre's characteristic framing devices: the closing rhetorical question 'So, AITA?' that caps a story before requesting judgment, and the verdict/judgment language that follows ('NTA', 'you're not the asshole', 'I think you're not entirely in the wrong', etc.). The top-activating examples are almost purely the literal tag-question 'So, AITA?' (or its variants 'am I the asshole', 'WIBTA'), while the broader cluster includes the surrounding advice-column moves of delivering a verdict, softening it with hedges, and offering supportive commentary. It is not merely about the topic of interpersonal conflict or moral wrongdoing in general -- it specifically captures the ritualized AITA request-for-judgment and judgment-delivery speech act, not generic apologies, complaints, or unrelated advice-giving that lacks this verdict structure. Sentences that discuss similar moral dilemmas but without invoking the AITA/NTA judgment framing (e.g. plain narrative description of a conflict) fall outside the core pattern.

title: Empathetic check-in questions
description: This latent fires on supportive, open-ended prompts that invite someone to share more about their feelings or situation, typically in emotionally sensitive or relational-advice contexts. Included sentences are short interrogatives like 'Is everything okay?', 'Can you tell me more about what happened?', 'What do you think?', and 'Would you like to talk about what's going on?' -- phrases whose function is to solicit disclosure, check emotional well-being, or gently open a conversation, often as sentence fragments or truncated stems ('Can', 'I know', 'Can I'). It is NOT about the surrounding advice-giving content, declarative explanations of feelings/motivations, statements of fact, or fully worked-out scripts/suggestions for what to say -- those (e.g. explaining why someone feels hurt, or advice like 'use I statements') fall outside this cluster even though they share the relationship-advice topic.

title: Self-care affirmation closer
description: This latent fires on formulaic, advice-column-style closing statements that tell the reader to prioritize themselves, take care of their own well-being, and affirm their inherent worth or deservingness of happiness. The highest-activating examples are near-templatic phrases like 'take care of yourself and prioritize your own well-being,' 'you deserve to be happy and fulfilled,' and 'remember to be kind to yourself,' often appearing as terminal or near-terminal sentences that wrap up a piece of relationship/emotional advice with a generic self-affirming imperative. It activates most strongly on the specific rhetorical formula of second-person imperative/affirmation ('remember,' 'take care,' 'you deserve') paired with abstract nouns like well-being, healing, growth, or happiness, regardless of the surrounding topic. It does NOT fire as strongly on other supportive or advice-giving sentences that lack this specific self-care/deserving-happiness phrasing -- e.g., sentences about boundaries, respecting others' autonomy, validating the reader's actions, or concrete situational advice (like 'seek counseling' or 'respect her decision') are only weakly represented, since the core pattern is the generic self-directed affirmation formula itself, not supportive advice in general.

title: Advice recommending mindfulness/relaxation practices
description: This latent fires on imperative or suggestion-style sentences that recommend specific stress-management or grounding techniques—especially mindfulness, meditation, deep breathing, yoga, progressive muscle relaxation, or guided imagery—as ways to stay present, calm, or centered. Top-activating examples are near-formulaic advice-list bullet points (often beginning with 'Practice,' 'Try,' or a bolded header) that enumerate these specific techniques, frequently in near-identical phrasing repeated across many outputs. It does not merely include any self-help or advice sentence: general advice about hobbies, social skills, confidence-building, communication, or goal-setting (seen in the random sample) is excluded unless it explicitly names a mindfulness/relaxation-type technique. The defining feature is the specific recommendation of calming/grounding practices, not advice-giving or self-improvement language in general.

title: Advice to have an open conversation
description: This latent fires on the recurring advice-giving template that tells the reader to resolve interpersonal conflict by initiating open, honest, calm, or respectful communication with another party (partner, family member, coworker, etc.). It activates most strongly on the stock phrases themselves -- 'By having an open and honest conversation,' 'Try to have a calm and respectful conversation,' 'By communicating openly' -- including truncated fragments like 'By' or '2.'/'3.' that appear as list markers introducing this exact suggestion. The cluster includes both the highest-activating bare templates and fuller sentences embedding the same recommendation (e.g., 'consider having an open and honest conversation with your girlfriend'), as well as closely related directives to listen, find common ground, or seek compromise as part of that conversation. It does NOT include other advice-column content such as apologizing, acknowledging feelings, reflecting on one's own behavior, suggesting third-party mediation, or general empathy statements, unless they are directly packaged as an instruction to 'have a conversation' -- i.e., the function is specifically the formulaic recommendation to talk things out openly, not communication or empathy as a broader theme.

title: Suggesting practical financial/logistical alternatives
description: This latent fires on sentences that propose concrete alternative arrangements or compromises for resolving a practical problem, typically financial, housing, transportation, or caregiving in nature -- e.g., 'explore alternative options,' 'consider a payment plan,' 'offer to contribute a smaller amount,' or 'find a more affordable option.' The top-activating examples are almost all advice-giving statements structured as suggestions or bullet points that recommend a specific fallback plan, compromise, or workaround (budgeting, refinancing, part-time jobs, alternative services, sliding-scale payments) in response to someone's stated problem. It is NOT simply about discussing money or relationships in general -- the random cluster examples that score lower involve evaluative or judgmental statements (assessing fairness, validating feelings, describing past behavior) rather than actively proposing a new option or solution. The defining feature is the act of offering/suggesting a concrete alternative course of action, not the topic of finances or interpersonal conflict itself.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens (e.g. '2.', '3.', '4.') that begin items in an enumerated or ordered list, typically within model outputs that present pros/cons, reasons, counterarguments, or step-by-step points. It activates specifically on the digit-plus-period marker itself, often followed by bold text or a list header like 'Here's why:' or 'Counterarguments', rather than on the content of the list item. It does not activate on prose sentences discussing similar topics (e.g. relationship advice, reasoning explanations) when they are not formatted as an enumerated list, nor on the first item '1.' as strongly as later numerals, nor on plain narrative sentences lacking list structure.
